concerns.text: The plan proposes using 'simulated DFT data' or 'RDKit/ForceField approximations' to generate spectra for USPTO reactions to train the model. This dataset strategy is inappropriate for the research question. The hypothesis (H1) claims 'spectroscopic data contains independent predictive signal.' Training a model on *simulated* spectra (which are deterministic functions of SMILES) and *real* yields creates a dataset where the spectral signal is perfectly collinear with the structural signal (ECFP4). The model cannot learn 'independent' signal because the simulated spectra contain no independent variance; they are just a different encoding of the SMILES. This renders the core scientific claim untestable with the proposed data source.

The plan acknowledges 'No single verified dataset contains all four fields' and pivots to 'simulated spectra' using 'random noise + functional group templates' or 'deterministic function of SMILES'. This confirms the dataset mismatch. A dataset where spectra are generated from SMILES (even with noise) does not represent the physical reality of experimental spectroscopy where yield depends on reaction conditions and subtle spectral features not captured by simple fingerprints. Using this data to claim 'independent predictive signal' is scientifically invalid (science-class issue manifesting as a methodology failure in data selection).

The plan states: 'If no verified spectral predictor exists, use random noise + functional group templates... to ensure the model has something to attend to'. This is a fabrication of data properties. Training on random noise or template-mapped noise does not validate the hypothesis that *real* spectroscopic data predicts yield. The dataset source (simulated/noise) is fundamentally wrong for the question. The plan must identify a real dataset with paired (SMILES, Experimental Spectrum, Yield) or explicitly pivot the research question to 'Can a model learn to map simulated spectra to yield?' (which is a different question).
